meta.indoorOutdoor: outdoor (open-water/pool swim + road/trainer bike + road/track run)
meta.contactLevel: none (open-water buoy contention + draft-legal pack contact aside)
meta.competitionFrequencyPerWeek: 0-1 races/week in season; an athlete targets 1-3 'A' races/year with B/C races as preparation
meta.notes: One continuous race across three disciplines (swim → T1 → bike → T2 → run). Demands scale enormously with distance — Sprint (~1h) to Ironman (8-17h) — so the engine should read the distance archetype (positions) rather than one split. The GYM is endurance SUPPORT: it improves economy, durability and (for the swim) shoulder health, and must never add fatigue that degrades the key swim/bike/run sessions or rob the legs before a long run. Two facts shape everything: the RUN is the highest-injury discipline (impact + it comes last, on fatigued legs), and the combined volume of three sports makes DURABILITY and energy availability the usual limiters, not the aerobic engine.

aerobicEndurance.why: The dominant determinant of performance across all three legs and every distance — the engine the whole race runs on.
aerobicEndurance.source: endurance physiology literature (Joyner & Coyle 2008); triathlon physiology (Millet 2009)

durability.why: Tissue tolerance to very high COMBINED weekly volume across three sports — in practice the limiter on how much an athlete can absorb, especially the run's repetitive impact.
durability.source: triathlon injury epidemiology (Vleck 2010; Andersen 2013); training-load literature

relativeStrength.why: Strength-to-mass drives power-to-weight for the run and the climb; neural strength supports economy WITHOUT adding non-propulsive mass to carry.

maxStrength.why: Underpins economy, durability and end-of-race/hill force, but triathlon is not max-strength limited — train it neurally (low volume) to avoid hypertrophy and interference.

explosivePower.why: Minor and intermittent — run finish kick, standing climbs, draft-legal surges; not a power sport.

reactiveStrength.why: Running is a stretch-shorten activity — lower-limb tendon stiffness improves running economy, the key trainable land quality for the run leg.
reactiveStrength.source: running-economy literature (Barnes & Kilding 2015); plyometric & economy reviews

sprintSpeed.why: Only the run finish and short draft-legal accelerations; the race is endurance-paced, so land sprint speed has low priority.

acceleration.why: Transitions, mounts/dismounts and draft-legal pack surges need brief acceleration; modest overall.

deceleration.why: Minimal braking demand — only dismount and turnarounds. Low priority.

changeOfDirection.why: Open-water buoy turns and bike cornering only; negligible land COD. Low priority.

anaerobicEndurance.why: Draft-legal short-course racing (bike pack surges + a flat-out run off the bike) and hill/finish efforts tax glycolytic capacity; far lower for steady non-drafting long course.

repeatSprintAbility.why: Draft-legal bike legs are stochastic — repeated accelerations out of corners and to hold the pack; irrelevant to non-drafting time-trial racing.

mobility.why: Multi-discipline range: shoulder/thoracic for the swim, ankle for swim kick + run, and hip range to hold an efficient aero position without low-back or hamstring cost.

stability.why: Hip/pelvic and trunk stability transfer force and protect tissues across single-leg running, the aero position, and the swim; instability drives run overuse and aero-position back pain.

rotationalPower.why: Long-axis body roll in the swim and trunk anti-rotation in running; otherwise low.

gripStrength.why: Forearm 'catch' in the swim aside, grip is not a limiter. Low priority.

neckStrength.why: Sustained cervical extension in the aero position and open-water sighting create low-grade neck demand; modest but real.

balance.why: Single-leg running stability, bike handling and open-water orientation; moderate.

coordination.why: Three distinct techniques plus transitions and the brick (running on bike-fatigued legs) make motor competence higher than for a single-sport endurance athlete.

energySystems.workToRestRatio: continuous across three disciplines (no rest — only transitions); event-dependent
energySystems.matchDemands: Overwhelmingly aerobic at every standard distance and progressively more so as distance rises. Sprint/draft-legal ≈ ~85% aerobic with meaningful glycolytic surges (bike pack + run finish); Olympic ≈ ~88-90%; 70.3 ≈ ~95%; Ironman ≈ ~98%+ aerobic, where fuelling and durability dominate over any high-intensity capacity. Values above are an Olympic-representative midpoint.
energySystems.heartRateProfile: Sustained high steady-state with discipline-transition spikes (notably the first minutes of the run off the bike); long-course is sub-threshold and pacing/fuelling-limited.
energySystems.fatigueProfile: Central + peripheral, CUMULATIVE across disciplines — fatigue carried out of the swim and bike degrades run mechanics (the cardinal triathlon failure mode); in long course, glycogen depletion and GI/fuelling limits dominate.
energySystems.source: triathlon physiology (Millet 2009; Bentley 2002); event-specific estimates vary — treat as indicative
energySystems.notes: Because the demand spans Sprint to Ironman, the engine should read the distance archetype (positions) rather than this single split.

planes: frontal (swim pull sweep, hip/pelvis control in run)
movementProfile.jointLoading: Repetitive shoulder load (swim); sustained flexed hip/spine load in the aero position (bike); high repetitive lower-limb impact through the ankle/knee/hip + bone (run) — the run is the dominant tissue-stress source.
movementProfile.groundContacts: Very HIGH during the run leg (repetitive impact is the central durability driver); none in the swim; none in the bike (the run is what breaks triathletes).
movementProfile.landingDemands: Continuous low-level landing/impact attenuation in running; dryland plyometrics add a deliberate, carefully dosed stiffness stimulus.
movementProfile.jumping: None in racing; only as a training stimulus (plyometrics for run economy).
movementProfile.rotating: Long-axis body roll in the swim (continuous); trunk anti-rotation in running.
movementProfile.overheadActions: Continuous during the swim leg (the source of swim-shoulder overuse), absent in bike/run.
movementProfile.collisions: None (incidental open-water and draft-legal pack contact aside).
movementProfile.repeatedImpacts: The run leg is high repetitive impact; swim and bike are low/no impact — so impact exposure is concentrated and comes LAST, on pre-fatigued legs.
movementProfile.asymmetricLoading: Breathing-side swim preference, left/right pedalling asymmetry and running gait asymmetry each accumulate across very high volume; bike-fit and gait asymmetries compound.
commonDeficiencies: posterior chain relative to quad dominance
hip/pelvic + trunk stability for single-leg running
scapular control + posterior cuff for swim volume
hip & thoracic mobility for the aero position

common.name: Running overuse — Achilles / calf tendinopathy
common.incidence: high (the run leg accounts for the majority of triathlon injuries)
common.mechanism: high repetitive impact and ankle plantarflexor load, frequently on legs pre-fatigued by the bike; run-volume spikes; reduced calf capacity
common.rtpConsiderations: Progressive calf-loading (isometric → heavy-slow → energy-storage), graded return to run volume, manage brick exposure.
common.source: triathlon injury epidemiology (Vleck 2010; Andersen 2013); Achilles tendinopathy literature (Alfredson; Silbernagel)

common.name: Patellofemoral pain (runner's / cyclist's knee)
common.incidence: high (both run impact and high pedalling volume load the patellofemoral joint)
common.mechanism: repetitive anterior-knee load; hip/quad weakness and poor frontal-plane control in running; high-cadence/high-volume cycling and bike-fit issues
common.rtpConsiderations: Hip/quad strengthening, load management across both run and bike, bike-fit review.

common.name: Bone stress injury / stress fracture (tibia, metatarsal, femoral neck)
common.incidence: moderate (run-driven; elevated where energy availability is low)
common.severity: high (significant time loss; femoral-neck is a medical emergency)
common.mechanism: repetitive bone loading outpacing remodelling; run-volume spikes; strongly amplified by low energy availability / RED-S, common given triathlon's huge volume and leanness pressure
common.rtpConsiderations: Medical management; address energy availability FIRST; very graded return to impact; never run through localised bony pain.

common.name: Swimmer's shoulder (subacromial / rotator-cuff)
common.incidence: moderate (lower swim volume than pure swimmers, but present)
common.mechanism: repetitive overhead swim loading; scapular dyskinesis and internal>external rotator imbalance; paddle/volume spikes
common.rtpConsiderations: Posterior-cuff + scapular strengthening, thoracic mobility, graded swim-volume return, reduce paddles.
common.source: Bak 2010; Sein 2010 (swimming shoulder, applied at lower triathlon swim volume)

common.name: Cycling-position low back & neck pain
common.mechanism: prolonged lumbar flexion + cervical extension in the aero/TT position; weak anti-extension and postural endurance; poor bike fit; compounded by run-derived lumbopelvic load
common.rtpConsiderations: Core endurance + mobility, progressive aero-position exposure, professional bike fit.

injuryProfile.summary: Overwhelmingly OVERUSE injuries spread across three disciplines, with the RUN the dominant source (impact, and it comes last on fatigued legs). The trainable levers are run-load management, lower-limb/calf capacity, hip-glute strength, swim-shoulder prehab, and aero-position core endurance. Bone stress + RED-S (low energy availability against very high combined volume) is the highest-severity risk and a fuelling-first problem, not only a training problem.

positions.name: Sprint distance (~750m / 20km / 5km)
positions.role: Shortest standard race — high relative intensity, often draft-legal at age-group/junior level.
positions.movementDemands: Near-threshold across all three legs; sharp run off the bike; transitions matter proportionally more.
positions.runningDemands: 5km flat-out off the bike — high relative running intensity.
positions.bodyComposition: Lean, higher tolerance of intensity; strong run.
positions.recoveryConsiderations: Higher intensity, lower absolute volume — tolerates a little more dryland power emphasis.

positions.name: Olympic / Standard (1.5km / 40km / 10km)
positions.role: The classic distance — draft-legal at elite/WTCS, non-drafting for most age-groupers.
positions.movementDemands: Sustained sub-threshold to threshold; the 10km run off the bike decides most races.
positions.runningDemands: 10km off the bike — run durability + economy are decisive.
positions.recoveryConsiderations: High combined load — strength placed away from key run/bike quality + long sessions.

positions.name: Middle / 70.3 (1.9km / 90km / 21.1km)
positions.role: Half-distance — sustained sub-threshold; pacing, fuelling and durability dominate.
positions.movementDemands: Long steady efforts; the half-marathon off the bike is a durability test.
positions.runningDemands: 21.1km off the bike on accumulated fatigue — durability is the limiter.
positions.recoveryConsiderations: Very high training volume — gym is low-volume support; protect the legs for long runs.

positions.name: Long / Ironman (3.8km / 180km / 42.2km)
positions.role: Full-distance endurance — 8-17h; fuelling, pacing and tissue durability are everything.
positions.movementDemands: Prolonged sub-threshold output; a marathon off the bike where mechanics degrade with fatigue and depletion.
positions.runningDemands: 42.2km off the bike — the ultimate durability + fuelling test.
positions.bodyComposition: Lean, highly efficient, robust to repetitive load.
gymPriorities: durability + tissue capacity (calf, hip, posterior chain)
positions.recoveryConsiderations: Highest volume + highest RED-S/bone-stress risk — fuelling and recovery are primary; gym is durability insurance, never a fatigue source.

positions.name: Draft-legal / short-course racer (WTCS / Olympic-distance elite)
positions.role: Pack-based, surge-heavy racing where the bike is stochastic and the run is a flat-out 10k off the bike.
positions.movementDemands: Repeated high-intensity bike surges + a fast run off the bike; transitions are decisive.
positions.runningDemands: Fast 5-10km off the bike at high relative intensity.
positions.bodyComposition: Lean-powerful; explosive for the run finish.
positions.recoveryConsiderations: Highest intensity profile — manage CNS/run-impact load; strength biased to power away from key brick sessions.

assessments.name: Discipline thresholds (bike FTP, run critical speed, swim CSS)
assessments.purpose: Individualise training zones for all three disciplines and track aerobic adaptation per leg.

targets.elite: improving power/speed at threshold; balanced across disciplines vs the athlete's weakest leg

assessments.name: Brick run-off-bike pace decoupling
assessments.purpose: Quantify how much run pace/economy degrades off the bike vs fresh — the signature triathlon quality.

assessments.name: Single-leg + calf capacity (heel-raise endurance, isometric calf)
assessments.purpose: Screen the lower-limb capacity that protects against the run's dominant overuse injuries (Achilles/calf, PFP).

targets.elite: high symmetrical calf endurance; balanced single-leg strength

assessments.name: Shoulder ER strength + mobility screen
assessments.purpose: Detect the internal>external rotator imbalance + ROM loss behind swimmer's shoulder.

assessments.name: Hip/ankle/thoracic mobility + aero-position screen
assessments.purpose: Confirm the range to hold an efficient aero position and run economically without compensatory low-back/hamstring cost.

targets.elite: holds aero with neutral spine; symmetrical hip/ankle ROM

assessments.name: Countermovement jump (CMJ)
assessments.purpose: Neuromuscular fatigue monitoring across heavy combined-load weeks + a coarse lower-limb power/stiffness proxy.

targets.elite: within ~10% of rolling baseline (fatigue); trend for power

equipment: jump mat / force plate / phone app

assessments.name: Energy availability / RED-S screen (incl. LEAF-Q where applicable)
assessments.purpose: Screen for low energy availability — the upstream driver of bone stress, hormonal disruption and stalled adaptation in high-volume triathletes.

targets.elite: adequate energy availability; normal menstrual function where applicable

youth.trainingEmphasis: Multi-sport literacy (swim/bike/run skills), fun, bodyweight + band strength and mobility; protect against early overuse from premature volume.

development.trainingEmphasis: Build the aerobic engine and tissue capacity (especially the run), establish a low-volume strength habit, embed fuelling + load tracking.

lowest: novel high-risk gym work in season
senior.trainingEmphasis: Individualised distance preparation; maintain strength/economy at low fatigue; protect the legs for key run/brick sessions; nail fuelling and the taper.

elite.trainingEmphasis: Data-led individualisation across three disciplines; precise concurrent-training sequencing; protect availability and energy availability.

masters.trainingEmphasis: Retain strength/power and mobility, manage run impact conservatively, allow longer recovery between key sessions.

offSeason.primaryObjective: Restore tissues; build the strength foundation and general aerobic base.
offSeason.trainingEmphasis: Aerobic base across disciplines, gym MAX-STRENGTH + tissue capacity (calf/hip/posterior chain), mobility, address the weakest discipline.

programming.source: triathlon S&C (Millet 2009): off-season rounds out the balanced physique; in-season is discipline-specific + prehab

preSeason.primaryObjective: Convert base to race-specific endurance + brick capacity.
preSeason.trainingEmphasis: Threshold + race-pace work, brick (run-off-bike) sessions, strength shifts to low-volume maintenance/power; mobility + prehab embedded.

programming.source: triathlon S&C (Millet 2009): off-season rounds out the balanced physique; in-season is discipline-specific + prehab

competition.trainingEmphasis: Race-specific sessions, maintained strength at minimal effective volume (away from key sessions), full prehab, careful run-load management.

programming.source: triathlon S&C (Millet 2009): off-season rounds out the balanced physique; in-season is discipline-specific + prehab

playoffs.primaryObjective: Peak for the A-race via a structured taper.
playoffs.trainingEmphasis: Reduced total volume (~40-60%) with maintained intensity; sharpening + race-pace primers; gym is priming/maintenance only; maximise recovery + fuelling.
testingRecommendations: readiness monitoring only — no fatiguing tests

recovery.primaryObjective: Physical + mental recovery; restore carried niggles; restore energy availability.
recovery.trainingEmphasis: Low/unstructured cross-training, mobility, light strength; rehab any carried Achilles/shoulder/back issues; rebuild fuelling.
testingRecommendations: none fatiguing; medical/dietary review of carried issues + energy availability

oneMatchPerWeek.pattern: A typical race-prep week built around the key endurance sessions (one quality bike, one quality/long run, one swim-quality, one long ride, plus the brick). Gym is placed to NOT fatigue the legs before the key run/brick or long ride.
oneMatchPerWeek.heavyDay: early-week, away from the key run/brick and long ride
oneMatchPerWeek.powerDay: mid-week low-volume power/plyometric (away from high run-volume days)
oneMatchPerWeek.recoveryDay: after the long ride/run + the day before a race
oneMatchPerWeek.injuryPreventionDay: calf + shoulder prehab embedded daily; primary strength dose early-week
oneMatchPerWeek.typicalLoadingPattern: Strength + base early → quality bike/run mid → brick → long session → easy/taper before race.
preferExplosiveWorkDays: mid-week power day away from high-impact run sessions

twoMatchesPerWeek.pattern: A race weekend or two races in a week: recovery-first; no heavy gym.
twoMatchesPerWeek.powerDay: brief race-morning priming only if used
twoMatchesPerWeek.typicalLoadingPattern: Race → recover → race → recover. Gym is priming/maintenance only.
avoidHeavyLiftingDays: all race days + the day before each

tournamentOrCongested.pattern: A multi-day stage event or a congested block of racing/travel: pure freshness + durability management.
tournamentOrCongested.typicalLoadingPattern: Protect the legs + fuelling between efforts; gym is priming, never development.

transfersWell: trap-bar deadlift (posterior chain, lower spinal load)
single-leg work — split squat / step-up (run-specific strength + durability)
single-leg calf raise (Achilles/calf capacity — run durability)
hip thrust / glute bridge (run power + durability)
pull-up / lat pulldown + rows (swim propulsion + shoulder balance)
band external rotation + scapular work (swim-shoulder prehab)
anti-rotation + anti-extension core (aero position + run posture)
limitedValue: high-volume hypertrophy / bodybuilding splits (adds non-propulsive mass to carry)
training to failure (excess fatigue interferes with key endurance sessions)
heavy barbell bench press (worsens swimmer's-shoulder internal-rotator dominance)
heavy strict overhead press (impingement risk in an overhead-loaded swim athlete)
long grinding strength sessions near key run/bike work
accessoryPriorities: core endurance for the aero position
gymPhilosophy.singleLegEmphasis: HIGH — running is a single-leg, repetitive-impact activity; single-leg strength, stability and calf capacity are central to both durability and economy. This is a key contrast with pool swimming.
gymPhilosophy.olympicLiftingSuitability: Optional/advanced — jumps + med-ball deliver most of the needed power/stiffness at lower technical and fatigue cost; not necessary for an endurance athlete.
gymPhilosophy.plyometricEmphasis: Moderate, carefully dosed — low-amplitude plyometrics improve running economy via tendon stiffness, but they add IMPACT to an athlete already impact-loaded by run volume; progress off a strength base and place away from high run-volume blocks.
gymPhilosophy.coreTrainingPhilosophy: Endurance + anti-rotation + anti-extension dominate: postural endurance to hold the aero position and stabilise the pelvis through tens of thousands of running strides; minimal high-volume flexion work.
gymPhilosophy.neckTraining: Low priority (low-dose tolerance work for the aero position only).
gymPhilosophy.rotationalTraining: Moderate — controlled anti-rotation supports swim body roll and running pelvic control; med-ball where useful.
gymPhilosophy.isometricTraining: Useful — tendon-friendly calf/quad isometrics for Achilles/PFP management, and low-fatigue strength + core holds in-season.
gymPhilosophy.tempoRecommendations: Controlled tempo for prehab/tendon work; heavy, low-rep, explosive-intent strength for economy (few reps, long rests, well short of failure); never grind near key endurance sessions.
gymPhilosophy.velocityRecommendations: Strength = high force, low volume, max intent; plyometrics = quality over quantity. The legs must be fresh for the run — quality and recovery beat gym volume.

warningSigns: calf/Achilles pain warming up then easing
exercisesToAvoid: high-amplitude plyometrics on a sore Achilles
injuryPreventionLibrary.source: Silbernagel; Alfredson (Achilles loading); triathlon injury epidemiology (Vleck 2010)

warningSigns: anterior knee pain on stairs/hills/after sitting
pain with high cycling volume or downhill running
exercisesToAvoid: deep loaded knee positions while symptomatic

warningSigns: localised bony pain on impact (worsening run-to-run)
injuryPreventionLibrary.recommendedFrequency: strength 2x/week + adequate fuelling + graded run progression
exercisesToAvoid: stacking volume on an under-fuelled athlete
monitoringRecommendations: weekly run-load + localised bone-pain check; medical referral on suspicion

decisionRules.if: run volume/impact ACWR > 1.5 (or a >~10-15% week-to-week run-load jump)
decisionRules.then: cap run volume this week, hold or reduce brick exposure, prioritise calf/lower-limb prehab; the run is the binding tissue ceiling
decisionRules.source: Gabbett 2016 (contested — Impellizzeri 2020, Lolli 2019); applied to run impact load

decisionRules.if: a key/long run or key brick session is scheduled within 24 hours
decisionRules.then: avoid heavy or high-soreness lower-body gym work the day before — preserve fresh legs for the run (the discipline that decides the race)

decisionRules.if: strength and a key endurance session fall on the same day
decisionRules.then: separate by the longest feasible window and run the priority quality first; lift for neural strength (low volume, short of failure) to minimise the interference effect
remove high-soreness gym (heavy strength, novel plyometrics, high-volume eccentric); allow only low-fatigue priming; cut endurance volume, keep some intensity

decisionRules.if: athlete reports shoulder pain on the swim pull OR ER strength drop >15% vs baseline
decisionRules.then: reduce swim pull/paddle volume + overhead gym; switch to pain-free scapular + ER prehab; flag for review

decisionRules.if: athlete reports localised bony pain on impact that worsens run-to-run
decisionRules.then: stop running on it, treat as suspected bone stress injury, refer medically, and screen energy availability — do NOT train through it

decisionRules.if: RED-S/low-energy-availability indicators present (under-fuelling, menstrual dysfunction, recurrent illness, stalled adaptation)
decisionRules.then: prioritise fuelling, reduce volume, refer to medical/dietetic support; do not chase volume or leanness

decisionRules.if: readiness score low (poor sleep + high soreness + low wellness)
decisionRules.then: autoregulate down one step; prioritise easy aerobic + recovery; do not test
treat as neuromuscular fatigue: reduce gym power/impact load, emphasise recovery, recheck
hold strength at minimal effective volume (1 low-volume session, high quality, away from key swim/bike/run sessions); maintain calf + shoulder prehab

decisionRules.if: athlete reports systemic illness (fever / below-neck symptoms)
decisionRules.then: withhold training until symptom-free; resume gradually

acwr.model: acute (7-day) : chronic (28-day) tracked PER DISCIPLINE (run impact, bike volume, swim volume) and as combined sRPE load; rolling/EWMA preferred. Run impact is the priority signal.
acwr.source: Gabbett 2016 applied per discipline — methodology contested (Impellizzeri 2020, Lolli 2019); soft monitoring input

loadManagement.weeklyProgressionGuideline: Avoid >~10-15% week-to-week spikes, especially in RUN volume — run impact is the load-limited tissue. Build the three disciplines' loads semi-independently.

gymVolumeRanges.offSeason: moderate-high (2-3 sessions; max strength + tissue capacity)
gymVolumeRanges.inSeason: low maintenance (1 session; low volume, high quality) + daily calf/shoulder prehab

loadManagement.minimumEffectiveVolume: ~1 low-volume strength session/week sustains strength/economy in-season; calf + shoulder prehab should not drop below a low ongoing dose.
loadManagement.maximumAdaptiveVolume: Off-season — build strength + tissue capacity + aerobic base here, while combined endurance volume is lower.
loadManagement.maximumRecoverableVolume: Constrained by TOTAL combined three-discipline load and lower-limb (run) tissue tolerance AND energy availability; gym must never compromise the key endurance sessions or the legs before the run — combined load + fuelling is the binding ceiling.
loadManagement.deloadRecommendations: Planned deload every 3-5 weeks in build phases; auto-deload on run-load ACWR >1.5, CMJ drop, red readiness, or any bone-stress/RED-S flag. The A-race taper is a planned, performance-oriented deload.
loadManagement.progressionRules: Progress a discipline (or gym) only when quality is met at target RPE, the relevant tissue is symptom-free, and energy availability is adequate; prefer intensity over volume in-season.
loadManagement.regressionRules: On run-tissue, shoulder or bone flags, or red readiness, drop the offending discipline's load (and gym volume) first; never schedule heavy legs the day before key run/brick work.
loadManagement.missedSessionRules: Do not stack missed sessions; resume at planned level. After time off (especially run or bone injury), rebuild run volume + impact gradually.
loadManagement.source: Bosquet/Mujika (taper); Gabbett (load — contested); Rønnestad & Mujika (maintenance); Mountjoy (RED-S); expert consensus

thresholds.when: calf/Achilles/knee soreness or localised bony pain
thresholds.modifier: cut run impact + heavy legs; prehab/mobility only; refer if bony pain

thresholds.when: under-fuelling signs vs very high volume
pain on swim pull or ER strength drop
thresholds.modifier: cut swim pull/paddles + overhead gym; prehab only
treat as accumulating fatigue; ease load

thresholds.when: racing block or long travel <48 h ago

readinessModel.notes: Lower-limb (run) soreness is elevated to a top-weight, triathlon-specific input — the run is the highest-injury discipline. Energy availability is included explicitly given the RED-S risk in high-volume triathlon. Subjective wellness + sleep + prior combined load carry the most general weight; objective vitals (HRV/RHR) are trend-only signals. Raw vitals stay private to the athlete; a coach sees only the derived readiness score (see TEAM-ARCHITECTURE.md).

coachDashboard.principle: Coach sees DERIVED and availability signals only — never an individual's raw HRV/sleep/resting-HR. Aggregated, plain-English, action-oriented.
mostUsefulKpis: high-risk athlete flags (run-load spike, bone-pain, shoulder)
coachDashboard.trafficLightIndicators: Per-athlete green/amber/red from the derived readiness + load state (no underlying numbers shown).
coachDashboard.privacyNote: All per-athlete entries here are DERIVED (readiness score, load_state, ACWR, adherence %, availability/RED-S status). Raw vitals are excluded by design and enforced by the schema validator.

strongEvidence: the taper improves performance — reduce volume, maintain intensity (Bosquet 2007; Mujika & Padilla)
heavy/explosive strength training improves running and cycling economy without added mass in endurance athletes (Rønnestad & Mujika 2014; Beattie 2017)
subjective wellness is a sensitive readiness measure (Saw 2016)
low energy availability drives bone stress injury + impaired health/performance (Mountjoy 2018)
weakEvidence: exact ACWR thresholds applied per discipline (contested)
precise event energy-system percentages by distance
magnitude of strength transfer to in-race triathlon performance specifically (vs single-sport economy studies)
CMJ as a precise performance predictor
plyometric dosing that improves economy without raising run-injury risk

balancing three disciplines against the athlete's weakest leg
areasRequiringFutureResearch: run-load monitoring thresholds in multi-discipline athletes
RED-S prevalence + management in age-group triathletes
long-term durability of high-volume multi-sport training
potentialRisksIfMisimplemented: heavy gym placed before key run/brick work, robbing the legs

kpis.eliteBenchmark: near-fresh run economy off the bike

kpis.name: Run threshold / critical speed
kpis.measurementMethod: Critical speed / threshold pace from time trials

kpis.name: Single-leg / calf capacity
kpis.measurementMethod: Single-leg heel-raise endurance + single-leg strength symmetry

kpis.name: Session RPE load
kpis.measurementMethod: RPE × duration across all disciplines + gym

kpis.name: Energy availability / RED-S status
kpis.measurementMethod: RED-S screen (LEAF-Q where applicable) + dietary/medical review — status only on shared surfaces

kpis.name: Resting HR
kpis.measurementMethod: Morning resting heart rate vs baseline
kpis.source: expert consensus (PRIVATE — athlete-only; rolls into readiness)

athleteDashboardKpis.name: Readiness
athleteDashboardKpis.why: One daily number telling the triathlete whether to push or back off across a heavy three-sport load.

athleteDashboardKpis.name: Weekly consistency
athleteDashboardKpis.why: Rewards showing up across a high-frequency, multi-discipline programme; consistency beats hero weeks.

athleteDashboardKpis.name: Performance trend (per discipline)
athleteDashboardKpis.why: Threshold/FTP/CSS improvement is the outcome the athlete trains for, shown per leg so the weakest is visible.

athleteDashboardKpis.name: Run-off-bike (brick) score
athleteDashboardKpis.why: The signature triathlon quality — a controllable margin the athlete can see improving.

athleteDashboardKpis.name: Lower-limb durability
athleteDashboardKpis.why: Turns invisible calf/hip prehab into a tracked score protecting the tissue that ends most triathletes' seasons.

athleteDashboardKpis.name: Mobility score
athleteDashboardKpis.why: Hip/ankle/shoulder range serves both economy and injury protection — reinforces the daily habit.

athleteDashboardKpis.name: Recovery / fuelling score
athleteDashboardKpis.why: Teaches that recovery and adequate fuelling (RED-S) are training, not optional.

athleteDashboardKpis.name: Availability streak
athleteDashboardKpis.why: Celebrates injury-free, training-able time across all three disciplines — framed positively.

coachDashboardKpis.name: Squad readiness
coachDashboardKpis.why: At-a-glance freshness (traffic-light, derived) to shape the session before it starts.

coachDashboardKpis.name: Training availability
coachDashboardKpis.why: Who is fit / modified / out (especially lower-limb) — the key planning input.

coachDashboardKpis.name: High-risk athlete flags
coachDashboardKpis.why: Surfaces athletes needing attention (run-load spike, bone-pain, shoulder, red readiness).

coachDashboardKpis.name: Per-discipline load distribution
coachDashboardKpis.why: Shows who is over/under-loaded in swim/bike/run to balance the week and protect the run.

coachDashboardKpis.name: Run-load ACWR distribution
coachDashboardKpis.why: Flags spike-risk athletes (soft input) on the highest-injury discipline.

coachDashboardKpis.name: Race readiness / taper status
coachDashboardKpis.why: Freshness picture into A-races — pacing + lineup decisions.

coachDashboardKpis.name: Training completion / compliance
coachDashboardKpis.why: Whether prescribed gym + prehab is actually being done.

coachDashboardKpis.name: Recovery trend (squad)
coachDashboardKpis.why: Derived readiness trend warns of accumulating fatigue across a block.

coachDashboardKpis.name: Injury/illness status summary
coachDashboardKpis.why: Availability picture (status only) for planning + medical liaison.

coachDashboardKpis.name: Energy-availability/RED-S flags
coachDashboardKpis.why: Surfaces the highest-severity, fuelling-driven risk (status only — never raw data).

coachDashboardKpis.name: Prehab compliance (calf + shoulder)
coachDashboardKpis.why: Whether the controllable injury levers are being pulled.

coachDashboardKpis.name: Fatigue distribution
coachDashboardKpis.why: Spread of green/amber/red shows if the whole squad or just individuals are cooked.

performanceScore.philosophy: Reflects progress toward the demands of the athlete's triathlon distance, weighted to aerobic capacity, durability and run-off-bike ability, rewarding consistency and availability and penalising excessive fatigue/poor recovery or low energy availability — never rewarding unsafe run loading or under-fuelling.

components.rationale: Consistency drives adaptation across a high-volume three-sport programme.
Injury-free (especially lower-limb) availability is the strongest performance lever in triathlon.
Threshold/FTP/CSS across disciplines is the core performance outcome.
Run-off-bike capacity is the decisive, controllable triathlon-specific margin.
Lower-limb tissue capacity is both protective and performance-relevant.
Range for aero position + run/swim economy and protection.
Strength underpins economy + durability without added mass.
Penalises chronic fatigue / poor recovery / low energy availability; keeps the score sustainable.

guardrails: never increases for training through localised bone/tendon pain, red readiness or injury
consistency + availability dominate so the score can't be gamed by occasional max efforts
low energy availability / poor recovery caps the score
does not reward adding mass or junk volume
performanceScore.explainability: Each component is shown with its contribution so the athlete sees why the score moved and what to work on next.

gamification.name: Injury-free weeks
gamification.rewards: Consecutive weeks available + completing calf/shoulder prehab — motivation tied to the sport's key injuries.

gamification.name: Consistency streak
gamification.rewards: Unbroken weeks hitting prescribed swim/bike/run + gym sessions; rewards process over outcome.

gamification.name: Prehab badge
gamification.rewards: Completing the calf + shoulder programme each week — makes the unglamorous work visible.

gamification.name: Brick milestone
gamification.rewards: Improving run-off-bike pace/decoupling — a triathlon-specific development goal.

gamification.name: Three-discipline balance
gamification.rewards: Bringing the weakest discipline up toward the others — rewards addressing the limiter.

gamification.name: Testing-battery completion
gamification.rewards: Completing each testing block (thresholds / calf capacity / CMJ / RED-S screen) — encourages objective tracking.

gamification.name: Personal-best milestones
gamification.rewards: Race-time + threshold PRs vs the athlete's own baseline — self-referenced, not leaderboard.
